blocks.text: An 86-year-old woman arrives for review carrying a carrier bag of eleven medicines. She cannot say what four of them are for. Her daughter says she has been dizzy and fell twice last month. Which of these medicines is she benefiting from, which is harming her, and what does she herself want from treatment?

blocks.markdown: Prescribing is not just choosing the right drug; it is agreeing with the patient what to take, and periodically agreeing what to stop. **Shared decision-making** is a process in which clinician and patient together consider the options, the likely benefits and harms and the patient's values, and reach a decision. The patient needs information in a form they can understand, and the clinician needs to learn what matters to the patient.

blocks.title: Absolute risk, relative risk and number needed to treat
blocks.text: **Absolute risk** is the proportion of people who experience an event over a stated time. **Absolute risk reduction (ARR)** is the control event rate minus the treated event rate. **Relative risk reduction (RRR)** is the ARR divided by the control event rate. **Number needed to treat (NNT)** is the number of patients who must be treated for one to benefit, the reciprocal of ARR. Relative figures sound larger and can mislead if the baseline risk is low.

blocks.caption: p_c is the event rate in controls and p_t in treated patients over the same period (expressed as fractions).

blocks.title: Converting trial results into patient language
blocks.prompt: In a 5-year trial of a preventive drug, 10 in 100 control patients and 7 in 100 treated patients have a stroke. Calculate ARR, RRR and NNT and express the result as a sentence for a patient.

steps.text: Patient wording: 'Out of 100 people like you, about 10 would have a stroke without the tablet and about 7 with it, so 3 of 100 avoid a stroke over 5 years, and about 97 of 100 get no stroke-prevention benefit, either because they would not have had one or still do.'

blocks.answer: ARR 3%, RRR 30%, NNT about 33. Natural frequencies and the absolute figures are clearer than '30% reduction'.

rows: Relative risk reduction only
'Reduces your risk by 30%'
Sounds large; hides baseline risk
Absolute risk (natural frequencies)
'3 fewer people in 100 have a stroke'
Easier to understand and compare
Harms with the same format
'1 more person in 100 has a major bleed'
Allows benefit and harm to be weighed on one scale
NNT
'33 people treated for 5 years to prevent one stroke'
Useful for clinicians, harder for some patients
blocks.caption: Presenting benefits and harms.

blocks.markdown: **Polypharmacy and inappropriate prescribing.** Polypharmacy usually means regular use of five or more medicines. It becomes problematic when drugs lack a current indication, duplicate one another, interact, or cause harm that outweighs benefit. Older adults are more vulnerable because of altered pharmacokinetics (reduced renal clearance, altered volume of distribution), frailty and limited life expectancy. Screening tools such as the STOPP/START criteria and the Beers criteria list **potentially inappropriate medicines**. A **prescribing cascade** occurs when an adverse effect is misread as a new condition and treated with another drug.

rows: Long-acting benzodiazepines or sedative hypnotics in an older adult
Confusion, falls and fractures
Strongly anticholinergic drugs (for example oxybutynin) in dementia or confusion
Worsen cognition, urinary retention, constipation
NSAIDs in chronic kidney disease, heart failure or with anticoagulants
Kidney injury, fluid retention, gastrointestinal bleeding
Proton pump inhibitor continued indefinitely without indication
Unnecessary exposure; infection and deficiency risks
Sulfonylurea with long half-life in frail patients
Prolonged hypoglycaemia
blocks.caption: Examples of potentially inappropriate prescribing in older adults (list illustrative).
Cockcroft-Gault estimate, with F = 1.23 for men and 1.04 for women; many drug doses in older adults are adjusted to it.

blocks.title: Estimating renal function before prescribing (teaching example)
blocks.prompt: A 78-year-old woman weighs 55 kg and has serum creatinine 110 micromol/L. Estimate her creatinine clearance.

steps.text: Substitute with F = 1.04 for a woman.

blocks.answer: About 32 mL/min, a clearly reduced value. Renally cleared drugs may need dose reduction or avoidance.

blocks.markdown: **Structured medication review.** A review is a systematic, patient-centred look at everything the patient takes, to optimise benefit and reduce harm. It starts with what the patient actually takes (including over-the-counter and herbal products), their understanding and goals, then examines each drug in turn.

items: Establish what the patient takes and how, and what matters to them
Check each drug has a clear current indication
Assess effectiveness: is the treatment goal being met?
Check safety: adverse effects, interactions, renal and hepatic function, falls risk
Check adherence and the burden of the regimen
Decide what to stop, reduce or simplify (deprescribing) and agree this with the patient
Plan monitoring and follow-up, and communicate changes to all carers

blocks.title: Deprescribing is a shared decision
blocks.text: Stopping a drug is a treatment decision like starting one. Explain why, involve the patient, stop one drug at a time when possible, monitor for withdrawal effects or return of symptoms, and document the decision.

points: Shared decisions use absolute risks in natural frequencies; ARR, RRR and NNT are linked, and benefits and harms should be presented in the same format.
Potentially inappropriate prescribing in older adults includes sedatives, anticholinergics and NSAIDs in at-risk patients, and prescribing cascades.
A structured medication review checks need, effectiveness, safety and burden, and agrees any deprescribing with the patient.

questions.stem: Which way of describing a benefit is generally easiest for patients to understand?

options.text: Natural frequencies, such as '3 fewer in 100 people'
A relative risk reduction expressed as a percentage only

questions.correctOptionText: Natural frequencies, such as '3 fewer in 100 people'

distractorRationale.b: This can exaggerate benefit when the baseline risk is low.
distractorRationale.c: This is difficult for most patients.
distractorRationale.d: A p-value does not describe the size of benefit.

questions.explanation: Natural frequencies and absolute risks allow patients to see how many people are affected. Presenting benefit and harm the same way supports a fair comparison.

questions.stem: A drug lowers the 5-year risk of a fracture from 2 in 1000 to 1 in 1000. Which statement best communicates the benefit?

options.text: It reduces the chance of a fracture from 2 in 1000 to 1 in 1000 over 5 years
It halves your risk, so it is certain to work
It prevents fractures in every patient
It is effective in 50% of patients

questions.correctOptionText: It reduces the chance of a fracture from 2 in 1000 to 1 in 1000 over 5 years

distractorRationale.a: Correct: gives absolute figures and time frame.
distractorRationale.b: 'Halves the risk' is true as a relative statement but omits the small absolute risk.
distractorRationale.c: Many patients would not have a fracture anyway.
distractorRationale.d: Misstates the meaning of relative reduction.

questions.explanation: The relative reduction is 50% but the absolute reduction is only 1 in 1000. Quoting the absolute change prevents overestimation of benefit.

questions.stem: Which medicine is most likely to be potentially inappropriate in an 84-year-old with recurrent falls?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: sedatives increase confusion, falls and fractures.
distractorRationale.b: This is not a classic cause of falls.
distractorRationale.c: This is not a classic cause of falls.
distractorRationale.d: Low fall risk at usual doses.

questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines impair balance and cognition in older adults and are listed in screening tools as potentially inappropriate, particularly with a falls history.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old starts a calcium channel blocker, develops ankle swelling and is then given a loop diuretic. What is this an example of?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: an adverse effect treated as a new condition.
distractorRationale.d: The swelling is a drug effect.

questions.explanation: Ankle oedema is a recognised effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. Treating it with a diuretic adds a drug and new risks; reviewing the original drug may remove the need.

questions.stem: What is the best first step in a structured medication review of a patient taking nine medicines?

options.text: Establish what the patient actually takes and what matters to them
Stop every medicine for a week
Add a further drug to cover all risks

questions.correctOptionText: Establish what the patient actually takes and what matters to them

distractorRationale.c: The aim is to reduce unnecessary drugs.

questions.explanation: A reliable review begins with what the patient actually takes, including over-the-counter items, and their goals. This avoids decisions based on an inaccurate list.

questions.stem: Deprescribing should involve the patient in the decision and include monitoring after a drug is stopped.
questions.explanation: Stopping a drug can unmask withdrawal effects or the return of the condition, so monitoring is needed. Patient involvement supports adherence and respects their preferences.

questions.stem: In a 3-year trial 8% of control patients and 6% of treated patients have an event. Calculate the number needed to treat to prevent one event.
questions.explanation: The absolute risk reduction is 0.08 minus 0.06, which is 0.02. The NNT is the reciprocal, 1/0.02, which is 50.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man weighs 60 kg and has a serum creatinine of 120 micromol/L. Estimate his creatinine clearance with the Cockcroft-Gault equation (factor 1.23 for men) in mL/min.
questions.explanation: The calculation is (140 - 82) x 60 x 1.23 divided by 120, which is 58 x 60 x 1.23 / 120 = 4280.4 / 120, about 35.7 mL/min. This reduced clearance matters for renally cleared drugs in older adults.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with 8% 10-year cardiovascular risk is offered a statin that the trial data suggest lowers relative risk by 25%. Explain how you would discuss benefits and harms in a way he can understand.
markingGuide: Convert relative reduction to absolute: 8% reduced by 25% is 2 percentage points (6% remaining)
Use natural frequencies, for example 2 fewer in 100 over 10 years
Present harms in the same format, such as muscle symptoms or small diabetes risk
Ask about values, concerns and preferences
Use plain language and check understanding with teach-back
Offer the option of not treating or lifestyle approaches
questions.explanation: The relative figure alone may overstate the benefit at a low baseline risk. Marking should reward absolute risk, format consistency and elicitation of patient values.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old woman takes ramipril, bisoprolol, ibuprofen, zopiclone, oxybutynin and omeprazole (started 6 years ago, no documented indication). She has chronic kidney disease and recent falls. Identify potentially inappropriate medicines and outline how you would conduct a structured medication review.
markingGuide: Ibuprofen with CKD and an ACE inhibitor: kidney risk and bleeding
Omeprazole without current indication to be reviewed
Start by confirming what she actually takes and her goals
Check indication, effectiveness, safety, adherence for each drug
Agree deprescribing with the patient, stagger changes and monitor
questions.explanation: The case combines high-risk drug-disease and drug-drug combinations. Marking should reward both identification and a structured, patient-centred plan.
